inference_aids.art_brief: Frame story, Scillus, early morning in spring, about 384 BC: in front of a whitewashed farmhouse doorway, a large clay wine amphora lies broken in several pieces in a dark red pool of spilled wine on the beaten earth. Philesia (about 35, dark hair bound up, blue-grey chiton and himation) stands over it with arms folded, grave and judge-like. On her right Gryllus (12, madder-red tunic) grins, plainly enjoying the trial; on her left Diodorus (10, woad-blue tunic, chestnut curls) stands very straight and looks at the ground. Sosias (old Thracian, grey beard, fox-skin cap, zigzag-banded cloak) crouches by the pieces and holds up a small wooden wax tablet dripping with wine. Xenophon (about 45, short greying beard, dark green cloak) leans in the doorway, dry and patient. A household servant in a plain tunic hovers behind. Painterly, consistent with the visual bible; no lettering, no vase pastiche.

grammar.note_en:
Athenaze left the perfect for later; Xenophon uses it constantly. The course has so far treated four perfects as vocabulary: οἶδα ‘I know’ (all through), δέδοικα ‘I am afraid’, ἕστηκε ‘is standing’, and τέθνηκε ‘is dead’. Each is the perfect of an act (seeing, dying, taking a stand, taking fright) and means the state that the act has left. That is the meaning this chapter illustrates: a past act seen from now, through the state it has produced.

The forms are easy to recognise. The stem is reduplicated: the first consonant is repeated with ε (ποιέω → πε-ποίη-κα, τρίβω → τέ-τριφ-α; a preverb stays in front, συν-τέ-τριφα, as the augment does). Stems that begin with a vowel lengthen it instead, and a few verbs repeat a whole syllable (ἀπ-ολ-ώλε-κα, Attic reduplication). After a vowel the ending is -κα; after a labial or guttural the consonant is often aspirated (β → φ in συντέτριφα); and a few common verbs have a ‘second perfect’ in plain -α (γέγονα, κατέαγα). The endings are -α, -ας, -ε(ν), -αμεν, -ατε, -ᾱσι(ν): like the first aorist’s endings except the third plural (-ᾱσι(ν), not -αν), and with no augment.

The narrow point of this chapter is the difference between the aorist and the perfect of the same verb, which English often blurs. When Philesia first sees the wine on the floor she asks Τίς τοῦτο ἐποίησεν; ‘Who did this?’ (s036): the aorist asks about the act, a single event in the past. When she turns to Diodorus she asks Τί πεποίηκας; ‘What have you done?’ (s052): the perfect asks about the act together with what it has left behind, the jar in pieces and the wine gone. His answer is in the same tense, Συντέτριφα αὐτόν, ‘I have smashed it’ (s053), and his mother’s Καὶ τὸν οἶνον ἀπολώλεκας, ‘and you have lost the wine’ (s058), is about a loss that still stands. Compare Sosias’s story of Tarsus, where a stone ἀμφορέα οἴνου συνέτριψεν, ‘smashed a jar of wine’ (s009): an event of long ago, told as an event, so aorist.

The second contrast is between two verbs. συντρίβω is transitive: someone smashes something, so συντέτριφα needs an object (αὐτόν). κατάγνυμι has an intransitive perfect: ὁ ἀμφορεὺς κατέαγεν means ‘the jar is broken’ (s034), and says nothing about who broke it. That is why the servant can report it without accusing anyone, and why the question who did it is still open. Its aorist is passive in form, κατεάγη, ‘broke, got broken’ (s055): Diodorus uses it for the moment of falling, the perfect is the state on the floor.

In Xenophon’s own text Cyrus asks Orontas φανερὸς γέγονας; ‘have you been shown up?’ (s102): γέγονα is the perfect of γίγνομαι, and the plot, once found, stays found. When you meet a perfect, strip the reduplication and the -κα or -α, look up the present, and translate with ‘has/have’ or with a present state (‘is broken’, ‘is dead’).

parergon.title: λαμβάνω τινὰ τῆς ζώνης: the genitive of the part taken hold of
parergon.body_en: Verbs of taking hold put the person in the accusative and the part grasped in the genitive: ἔλαβον τὸν Ὀρόνταν τῆς ζώνης (s109), ‘they took Orontas by the belt’; Gryllus does the same to his brother, τὸν Διόδωρον τῆς ζώνης ἔλαβεν (s120), ‘took Diodorus by the belt’. The genitive is partitive: they hold not all of him but part. With the middle ἔχομαι ‘cling to’ the thing held is genitive by itself: τῶν σκευοφόρων εἰχόμεθα (s077), ‘we held on to the baggage animals’.

pair.sense_grc: συγκαλέω: πολλοὺς εἰς ἓν καλῶ · «ἡ δὲ Φιλησία πάντας πρὸ τῆς οἰκίας συνεκάλεσεν»
παρακαλέω: τινὰ παρ’ ἐμαυτὸν καλῶ · «ἡ δὲ Φιλησία τὸν Σωσίαν παρεκάλεσεν»
pair.sense_en: summon (to one’s side); also call on, encourage

families.spelling_note: Both are καλέω ‘call’ with a preverb. σύν becomes συγ- before κ (συγ-καλέω), but before the augment the ν comes back: συν-ε-κάλεσεν (s013, s037, s084). παρά loses its α before the augment: παρ-ε-κάλει (s022), παρ-ε-κάλεσεν (s044, s087); Cyrus’s own παρεκάλεσα ὑμᾶς (s093). The difference is the direction: συγκαλεῖν is to call many people together to one place, as Clearchus called his soldiers and Philesia her household; παρακαλεῖν is to call someone (one or several) to your side, as Cyrus summoned Clearchus and Philesia summoned Sosias to look. παρακαλέω also has a sense that is not simply ‘call beside’: ‘call on someone to act, encourage’; it is common later in the Anabasis. The diagram shows the two directions.
